faqs.a: Binary (base 2) is how computers count with on/off signals, and hexadecimal (base 16) is a compact shorthand engineers use because one hex digit holds exactly four bits.
faqs.q: What are base 2 and base 16 used for?

faqs.a: We have 10 digit symbols plus 26 letters, which gives 36 symbols in total: 0–9 then A–Z.
faqs.q: Why do bases go up to 36?

faqs.a: Group the bits in fours from the right, then turn each group into one hex digit. 101111 becomes 10 1111, which is 2 F.

howItWorks: Every positional number system works the same way: each digit is worth its face value times the base raised to its position. Base 10 is just the one we happen to use — base 2 uses only 0 and 1, base 8 uses 0–7, and base 16 uses 0–9 plus A–F for the values 10–15. Converting between two bases therefore goes through decimal as a convenient middle step: first expand the number by place value to get its decimal value, then repeatedly divide by the target base and collect the remainders.

The digits for values above 9 are the letters A to Z, so base 36 is the largest base with single-character digits. Before converting, the calculator checks that every digit you typed is legal in the from-base — a 2 is not a binary digit, and a 9 is not an octal digit — and rejects the input with a clear message if not.
intro: Convert a number between any two bases from 2 (binary) to 36. Type the number, tell us which base it is written in and which base you want, and see every step of the conversion.

mistakes.text: Every base has exactly that many digits starting from 0. Binary digits are only 0 and 1, octal digits are 0–7. A 2 in a binary number is always a typo.
mistakes.title: Using a digit the base does not have

mistakes.text: The first remainder you find is the rightmost digit. Read the column of remainders from the last division up to the first.
mistakes.title: Reading the remainders top to bottom

mistakes.text: In bases above 10, letters are digits with real values: in hexadecimal A = 10 through F = 15. So 1A in hex is 1 × 16 + 10 = 26, not 'one-A'.
mistakes.title: Forgetting that letters are digits

mistakes.text: Going to decimal multiplies each digit by powers of the base; coming from decimal divides by the new base. Mixing the two directions up gives nonsense.
mistakes.title: Mixing up the direction
